newsitem.title: CHINA: China PC demand booming, competition fierce.
newsitem.headline: China PC demand booming, competition fierce.

text.p: China's demand for personal computers is booming and competition is fierce as domestic producers cut prices to grab market share, computer producers said on Friday.
Demand was growing 70 to 80 percent a year, said producers at the country's largest annual computer exhibition being held in Shanghai this week.
Sales of personal computers in China are expected to reach three million in 1997, up from 1.8 million in 1996, according to official forecasts.
Despite solid growth, the proportion of families that own PCs in China's booming coastal cities now stood at only five percent, leaving further room for the market to develop, producers said.
"China's computer market has huge potential, but the competition is fierce because everyone wants a slice of the cake," said an official of one computer company.
Competition has been heightened by local producers cutting prices to unseat well known foreign companies including IBM Corp and Compaq Computer Corp
"Domestic producers are grabbing more and more market share from foreign companies," said a sales manager with Tontru Group, one of China's major PC producers.
"In 1995, China's name-brand computer producers had a total market share of 16 percent, and that figure increased to 27 percent in 1996," he said.

One analyst said foreign companies now had one-third of the PC market, down from around 40 percent last year. The remaining market share was taken up by "no-name" computers, often assembled by technicians to order.
"The quality of domestically made computers has improved a lot and prices have fallen, making them more attractive to individual buyers," the analyst said.
Legend, China's biggest PC maker, seized 10 percent of the market with sales of 200,000 computers last year, double the number of its PCs sold in 1995, company officials said.
"Our target for 1997 is to sell 400,000 computers," a Legend official said.
Legend began cutting prices in February, which has led to discounts of up to 50 percent from comparable foreign brand PCs, the official media has reported.
Analysts said the acceptable price ceiling for a new personal computer for individual use was around 10,000 yuan ($1,205), but foreign brands were usually 20 or 30 percent higher.
But the lower prices have a downside. Increased competition means narrower profit margins.

"We can only make one to three hundred yuan with a computer priced at 10,000 yuan," a local sales manager said. "Profit margins have fallen sharply since producers began cutting prices to compete for market share."
